title: Cap. VIII: Hactenus Jesuitarum — turn to Corvinus; negative reprobation to liberty alone
latin: Hactenus Jesuitarum ac Scholasticorum argumenta ventilavimus. Urgentur et alia nonnulla a Corvino, in Defensione sententiae Arminianae adversus Tilenum: in quibus si quid occurrat novi, diluetur. Eo autem magis nobis laborandum est, ut reprobationis actum negativum, quem praeteritionem sive non-electionem vocare possumus, ad solam Divinae voluntatis libertatem revocemus, quia omnes qui hanc reprobationem ex praevisione actuum malorum deducunt, electionem etiam ex praevisione actuum bonorum suspendunt.
pass_a: Thus far we have ventilated the arguments of the Jesuits and of the Scholastics. Certain others also are urged by Corvinus, in the Defense of the Arminian sentence against Tilenus: in which if anything new occur, it shall be washed away. But so much the more must we labor, that we may recall the negative act of reprobation, which we can call passing by or non-election, unto the sole liberty of the Divine will, because all who deduce this reprobation from foresight of evil acts also suspend election from foresight of good acts.
pass_b: So far we have aired the Jesuits' and Scholastics' arguments. Corvinus also presses others in his Defense of the Arminian sentence against Tilenus — and if anything new appears there, it will be cleared. We must labor all the more to recall the negative act of reprobation — which we may call praeterition or non-election — to the sole liberty of the divine will. For all who derive this reprobation from foresight of evil acts also hang election on foresight of good acts.

title: Cap. VIII: Augustine rejects foresight of Esau's evil and Jacob's good alike as causes
latin: Huc etiam accedit quod Augustinus (quo nemo doctius aut sanctius hanc causam tractavit) tam negat praevisa mala opera Esavi fuisse causam quod a Deo reprobaretur, quam praevisa bona opera Jacobi negat causam fuisse quod is a Deo eligeretur. Videte Enchir. ad Laurent. cap. 98, Ad Simpl. lib. 1. quaest. 2, et Epist. 105, ubi illorum sententiam qui inquiunt Deum nondum natorum vel hunc odisse vel illum dilexisse, quia eorum futura opera praevidebat, ex aequo rejicit. Et Epist. 106 aperte docet, Deum diligendo eos discernere, quos merita nulla discernunt. Sicut igitur praevisionem bonorum meritorum non admittit causam fuisse electionis, ita nec praevisionem malorum concedit fuisse rationem reprobationis. Nam ubi ex una parte considerantur boni actus, puta credendi, obediendi, perseverandi, ex altera mali actus hisce oppositi, illos ut meritis discretos considerari perspicuum est. Sed ad Corvini sententiam veniamus.
pass_a: To this also is added that Augustine (than whom no one treated this cause more learnedly or more holily) as much denies that the foresighted evil works of Esau were the cause that he was reprobated by God, as he denies that the foresighted good works of Jacob were the cause that he was elected by God. See the Enchiridion to Laurentius chapter 98, To Simplicianus book 1 question 2, and Epistle 105, where he equally rejects the sentence of those who say that God hated this one or loved that one of those not yet born, because he foresaw their future works. And Epistle 106 openly teaches that God by loving discerns those whom no merits discern. As therefore he does not admit foresight of good merits to have been the cause of election, so neither does he grant foresight of evils to have been the reason of reprobation. For where on one side good acts are considered, for example of believing, of obeying, of persevering, on the other evil acts opposite to these, it is clear that those are considered as discerned by merits. But let us come unto the sentence of Corvinus.
pass_b: Add Augustine — no one treated this cause more learnedly or holily: he denies as much that Esau's foresighted evil works were the cause of his reprobation as that Jacob's foresighted good works were the cause of his election. See Enchiridion to Laurentius 98, To Simplicianus 1.2, and Epistle 105, where he equally rejects those who say God hated or loved the not-yet-born because he foresaw their future works. Epistle 106 openly teaches that God by loving discerns those whom no merits discern. As he will not admit foresight of good merits as election's cause, so he will not grant foresight of evils as reprobation's reason. For where good acts — believing, obeying, persevering — stand on one side and opposite evil acts on the other, those are clearly regarded as discerned by merits. But let us come to Corvinus's sentence.

lemmas.gloss: God discerns by loving, not by merits

title: Cap. VIII: Corvinus with Arminius — reprobation only from personal rejection of offered grace
latin: Is igitur cum Arminio statuit, Deum singulares personas semper reprobare ex personali earundem propria gratiae oblatae rejectione; ita ut nec in decreto reprobationis quenquam rejecerit aut praeterierit nisi consideratum ut actu infidelem et impenitentem contra Deum actu vocantem, nec in Adae lapsu quenquam ex absoluta sua ordinatione reliquerit, aut propter solum originale peccatum damnare decreverit.
pass_a: He therefore with Arminius establishes that God always reprobates singular persons from their own personal rejection of offered grace; so that neither in the decree of reprobation has he rejected or passed by anyone except considered as actually unbelieving and impenitent against God actually calling, nor in the fall of Adam has he left anyone from his absolute ordination, or decreed to damn on account of original sin alone.
pass_b: With Arminius he therefore holds this: God always reprobates particular persons from their own personal rejection of offered grace. In the reprobation decree, on that view, he has rejected or passed by no one except as actually unbelieving and impenitent against God who is actually calling. Nor in Adam's fall has he left anyone by absolute ordination alone, or decreed to damn for original sin only.

lemmas.gloss: reprobation from personal rejection of offered grace
deny damnation for original sin alone

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: personal unworthiness foresighted — but not antecedent motive of the reprobation decree
latin: In hac sententia, si de adultis solis sermo sit, concedemus Arminio et Corvino, personalem ac propriam quandam indignitatem, ex voluntaria rebellione ortam, fuisse in illis omnibus ab aeterno praevisam, quos Deus ab aeterno reprobavit: sed negabimus, ex praevisa hac actuali et finali eorundem rebellione decretum reprobationis, tanquam ex causa antecedanea et motiva, emanasse. Quin potius affirmamus, in voluntate Divina prius concipi a nobis oportere decretum illud indurationis permissivae sive reprobationis, de qua Apostolus sic loquitur, Miserebitur cujus vult, et quem vult indurat, quam in mente Divina concipere possimus praevisionem istam ad quamlibet singularem personam relatam, qua ab aeterno Deus intuetur eandem personam ut gratiae suae reluctantem, et ad finem usque vitae suae eandem gratiam contumaciter aspernantem et rejicientem.
pass_a: In this sentence, if speech be only of adults, we will concede to Arminius and Corvinus that a certain personal and proper unworthiness, sprung from voluntary rebellion, was foresighted from eternity in all those whom God from eternity reprobated: but we will deny that from this foresighted actual and final rebellion of the same the decree of reprobation flowed as from an antecedent and moving cause. Nay rather we affirm that in the Divine will that decree of permissive hardening or of reprobation, of which the Apostle so speaks, He will have mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens, ought to be conceived by us prior, before we can conceive in the Divine mind that foresight related unto any singular person, by which from eternity God regards the same person as struggling against his grace, and unto the end of his life contumaciously spurning and rejecting the same grace.
pass_b: If the talk is of adults only, we grant Arminius and Corvinus this much: a certain personal proper unworthiness, sprung from voluntary rebellion, was foresighted from eternity in all whom God from eternity reprobated. What we deny is that from that foresighted actual and final rebellion the reprobation decree flowed as from an antecedent moving cause. Rather we affirm: in the divine will we must first conceive that decree of permissive hardening or reprobation of which Paul speaks — He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens — before we can conceive in the divine mind that foresight of any particular person as from eternity struggling against his grace and, to life's end, contumaciously spurning and rejecting it.

lemmas.gloss: foresight unworthiness yes; motive cause no
hardening decree prior to foresight of resistance

title: Cap. VIII critique: Corvinus's vocabulary of unbelief and vocation against Scripture; original sin alone
latin: Porro, quando in constituenda sua sententia dicunt, Deum in decreto reprobationis considerare homines ut actu infideles et impenitentes contra Deum actu vocantem, coguntur vocabulis uti contra receptam sacrarum Scripturarum et omnium fere Theologorum consuetudinem. Si enim norman loquendi a Scripturis et sanis Theologis accipere velimus, infidelitas denotat rejectionem Evangelii, et vocabula gratiae ac vocationis Evangelii patefactionem praesupponunt. At Arminio et Corvino ob infidelitatem praevisam reprobantur, quibus Evangelium nunquam fuit annuntiatum; gratiam ac vocationem rejecisse dicuntur, quibus gratia Christi nunquam fuit oblata. Denique, quod de originali peccato docent, illud haud facere ullum hominem aeternae mortis reum, nec propter illud solum quenquam damnari, hoc profecto tam alienum est a catholicae Ecclesiae doctrina, quam est cum Arminiana Theologia necessario conjunctum et connexum.
pass_a: Further, when in constituting their sentence they say that God in the decree of reprobation considers men as actually unbelieving and impenitent against God actually calling, they are compelled to use vocabularies against the received custom of the sacred Scriptures and of almost all Theologians. For if we will take the norm of speaking from the Scriptures and from sound Theologians, unbelief denotes rejection of the Gospel, and the vocabularies of grace and of vocation presuppose the manifestation of the Gospel. But by Arminius and Corvinus they are reprobated on account of foresighted unbelief, to whom the Gospel was never announced; they are said to have rejected grace and vocation, to whom the grace of Christ was never offered. Finally, what they teach concerning original sin, that it by no means makes any man guilty of eternal death, nor that anyone is damned on account of that alone, this truly is as alien from the doctrine of the catholic Church as it is necessarily conjoined and connected with Arminian Theology.
pass_b: Further: when they say that in the reprobation decree God considers men as actually unbelieving and impenitent against God actually calling, they are forced to use words against the received custom of Scripture and of almost all theologians. If we take our speaking-norm from Scripture and sound theologians, unbelief denotes rejection of the Gospel, and the words grace and vocation presuppose the Gospel's manifestation. Yet on Arminius's and Corvinus's view, people are reprobated for foresighted unbelief to whom the Gospel was never announced, and said to have rejected grace and vocation to whom Christ's grace was never offered. Finally, their teaching that original sin makes no man guilty of eternal death, and that no one is damned for that alone, is as alien to the catholic Church's doctrine as it is necessarily bound up with Arminian theology.

lemmas.gloss: denying damnation for original alone vs catholic doctrine

title: Cap. VIII close into Cap. IX: Corvinus's arguments to be proposed and dissolved
latin: Verum ad argumenta istorum proponenda et diluenda accingamur. Cap. IX. Corvini argumenta proponuntur et diluuntur.
pass_a: But let us gird ourselves unto proposing and washing away the arguments of these. Chapter IX. The arguments of Corvinus are proposed and dissolved.
pass_b: But let us now gird ourselves to propose and dissolve their arguments. Chapter IX — Corvinus's arguments proposed and dissolved.

lemmas.gloss: turn from Cap. VIII close to Cap. IX Corvinus args
